research_scope: Only the seven bound target keywords; no topic reselection.

findings.statement: Training poles should be supported so that they can fall readily when struck; in FEI schooling areas poles must be in cups at both ends, in a cup at one end with the other on the ground, or fully on the ground.
Selection should consider material, weight, visibility, intact surfaces without splinters or sharp edges, compatible supports and practical storage.
Ground lines, when used, have defined safe placement relative to the obstacle; schooling setup should account for horse and rider ability.
Good arena lighting aims for even visibility and avoids glare, hard shadows and strong brightness transitions.
Mounting position and height influence whether corners and track are illuminated; outdoor installations must account for weather and electrical safety.
Where a suitable adjacent building exists, luminaires can sometimes be mounted on the building instead of dedicated high masts; photometric suitability still depends on geometry and mounting height.
Container volume should match actual manure volume and realistic collection frequency; access and turning space for the collection vehicle are part of the selection.
A lid or sheltered position can reduce added rainwater; doors, flaps, edges and filling height must remain practical and safe in daily use.

Manure storage must prevent uncontrolled leachate and comply with local water and agricultural requirements; covered or watertight container solutions can be relevant depending on the site and local rules.
German Civil Code §833 establishes liability of an animal keeper when the animal injures a person or damages property, subject to the statutory wording and exceptions.
A foreign or guest rider is commonly distinguished from a regular riding participation; policy wording should explicitly address the actual use.
Insurance products differ in whether riding participations, foreign riders, noncommercial keepers and other situations are included; commercial use may be excluded in consumer tariffs.
Selection should compare insured persons and situations, limits, deductible and exclusions rather than price alone.
Healthy hoof horn needs an appropriate moisture balance; much of the moisture of a healthy hoof comes from within.
Persistently wet and dirty conditions can damage the hoof's natural protective layers; topical dressings are supportive care rather than a substitute for trimming and management.
Huffett choice should depend on hoof condition, housing and environment; cleaning before application and professional assessment of heat, deep cracks or abnormal smell are important.
Fly masks are intended to protect eyes and face from insects; some products additionally claim UV protection.
Fit is critical: the mask should remain clear of the eyes, avoid rubbing and be checked regularly for dirt, moisture and shifting.
Ear or nose coverage should be selected according to the horse's actual need; secure closures and clean, dry material matter in daily use.
Pelleted feeds can differ greatly by purpose and formulation; forage-based pellets can be useful for horses with poor dentition and may need soaking for some horses.
Pelleted complete feeds can offer uniform intake and lower dust but may increase choke risk and reduce long-stem fibre if used inappropriately.
Feeds designed to absorb substantial water, such as some sugar-beet products, must be prepared according to soaking instructions because incomplete soaking can contribute to choke.
Selection should be based on recipe, role in the total ration, weighed quantity, storage quality and manufacturer preparation instructions rather than pellet appearance.
